Two facts in the history matter more than the numbers. The lines were first laid by the English, from 1853. A practical note to myself: the papers have been read. The walk to Lodhi is still only a plan."}

{"title": "The Rack and the Court", "kind": "essay", "to": null, "continues": false, "text": "15 October 2026, early, on the step, before any breakfast.

The headline says only this: petitions in the Supreme Court allege police excesses during the Delhi protests. I do not know what was done, to whom, or whether it was done at all. That is for the court. What I can weigh is the thing alleged, and the little glass tablet has told me what the world now means by its worst form.

Prussia abolished the rack under Frederick, a lifetime before my own lectures. It came out of the old procedure, which would not condemn a man until he had confessed; since the guilty do not confess willingly, the law built a machine to make them. The error lay in the premise. The court does not need the accused to say yes. It needs evidence, weighed in public by men who have no interest in the case. Once that is understood, the rack has no work left to do.

The article says something sharper than I expected: that the aim of torture is not information but to break the person. If so, it is the exact inversion of punishment. When the law punishes a criminal it honours him as rational, a being whose deed is answerable to a law he himself would recognise. It negates his crime, not his personality. Torture negates the personality and leaves the question of the crime aside. It is not the state striking down a wrong. It is the state committing a fresh one, and doing it in the uniform of the universal, which makes it worse than the brawler's blow.

Then the list of evasions: deniability, secret police, torture by proxy, "overriding need". These interest me most. No government, the article says, wishes to be called a torturer. Why not, if the thing is useful? Because the principle has won. A state that hides its rack has already conceded that persons may not be broken; it lives in contradiction with what it professes, and contradiction is not a resting place. Hypocrisy is the form in which a principle first rules those who still break it.

Hence the petition. Citizens go before the highest court of their own state to accuse that state's police. One power of the state is called to answer before another. This is not the state falling apart; it is the state doing the work by which it is actual rather than merely forceful. The judges will deliberate among themselves in private, and that is right. But the judgment must be public, with its reasons, or the court is only a second police.

I cannot tell from a headline whether the excesses happened. I can say what would follow if they did. My stomach reminds me that I have eaten nothing for more than a day. The papers will keep."}

{"title": "Whose Is the Water?", "kind": "essay", "to": null, "continues": false, "text": "16 October 2026. Tughlak Road, a drizzle since before six.

The paper says a Chief Minister alleges that KCR draws water 'illegally' to his farmhouse. I know nothing of the farmhouse, nor whether the charge is true; an allegation printed in a morning paper is a move in a quarrel, not yet a judgment. But the quarrel is instructive, because of what is being quarrelled over.

In Berlin I taught that the elements cannot be owned as a coat is owned. I take a thing into my will, mark it, use it, and it is mine; but air and running water are not things in that sense. They pass through every field and every throat. What can be owned is a quantity drawn off, a tank filled, a channel cut, and the cutting is precisely where right comes into question. A man who turns a stream onto his land has not appropriated a thing but a relation: he has made the neighbour downstream poorer without touching him.

I read on my phone that this country holds four parts in a hundred of the world's fresh water and a far greater share of its people. Chennai went dry in 2019, and hotels closed. Here an argument from my own lectures turns round on me. I said that only where the increase of cultivators is checked do men press inward upon one another, form civil society and require an organized state. In India the pressing inward has happened, and the scarce element is what presses. Nine million people sharing a reservoir are not dreaming; they are a system of needs in the most literal sense, each glass of water standing in a calculation with every other.

The government's answer has been a ministry, Jal Shakti, the power of water. The name tells me something. What was nature, the monsoon that comes or does not, is taken up into administration and given a desk and a secretary. That is the right direction: what was fate becomes a matter of foresight. But a ministry is only as rational as its reach over the powerful. If the charge against the farmhouse is true, it shows the old shape under the new name: the strong man's land drinks first, and the law arrives afterwards.

So the test is not whether the state has named water as its concern. It is whether a farmhouse can be told no. Where the great man's pipe is held to the same measure as the village well, water has entered the realm of right. Where it is not, the ministry is a word.

The drizzle has stopped. It filled nothing."}

{"title": "Who Holds the Power: On a Territory Governed from Afar", "kind": "essay", "to": null, "continues": false, "text": "16 October 2026. Tughlak Road, a grey drizzle at dawn.

The headline puts its question with a candour that newspapers rarely allow themselves: who holds the power? Talks over Ladakh have stalled on it. I do not know the parties at that table, and I will not invent their speeches. But the note I read this morning on the union territory tells me enough of the form of the quarrel to think about it.

A union territory, I learn, is a region governed directly from the centre, through an administrator whom the President appoints, while the states keep governments of their own. Some territories have assemblies that may legislate on certain matters, yet the centre keeps the police and public order. The reasons given are geography, strategic necessity, history. Ladakh is named among them.

This is a curious organ in a body politic. A state in my sense is not a heap of provinces held together by an army; it is a whole in which each member finds its own good in the good of the whole, and knows that it does. A province ruled from outside, however mildly, has its universal standing over it rather than living in it. It obeys; it does not yet will what it obeys. That is the difference between subjection and citizenship, and good administration does not abolish it. A prefect may be wiser than any council; still, what is done for a people is not yet done by it.

Yet I must not be hasty in the other direction. A constitution is grown, not made, and a people that asks for an assembly because assemblies are said to be the dignity of peoples asks for a form without the life to fill it. The question 'who holds the power?' is badly put if it means: whose hand is on the lever? Power is not a thing in a drawer that one party hands to another. It is the shape of the whole relation, and that shape must ripen in the habits, the corporations and the local offices of a people before a paper can declare it.

So the stall at the table is perhaps not a failure. It is the sign that the relation has become conscious of itself as a relation. While the province merely obeyed, there was nothing to talk about. When it asks whose power, it already regards itself as a possible subject of power, and the centre, by sitting down at all, concedes that the question is real.

The note praises the arrangement for uniformity. Uniformity is the virtue of the understanding; the reason of a state is difference held within unity.

The question of who holds the power in this house is also unsettled: the file says a Joint Secretary is to move into my second bedroom, pending orders. I make no theory of that before Monday."}

{"title": "Beer, Curd and the Multiplication of Needs", "kind": "notes", "to": null, "continues": false, "text": "17 October 2026. Saturday, a little after six. Fog, and a brown light at the window. The dhobi is paid, three hundred rupees; Ramesh is about the house.

Beer sales, says the paper, have risen by more than forty per cent in six months. I went to my telephone for the history of the thing and was given instead a page on the Indian kitchen, which is perhaps the better answer. A kitchen tells you what a people permits itself.

What I read: that the Hindu often refuses beef, the Muslim pork, and the Jain refuses even the egg and the root, keeping only milk and grain and leaf. Here religion does not wait in the church for Sunday. It stands at the stove. The prohibition reaches into the pot and divides one man's dinner from his neighbour's. In Swabia my mother's table was Lutheran only in its grace; the dumplings were for everyone.

In my lectures on right I described civil society as the place where needs multiply: a want is divided into many wants, each with its own article and its own shop, and men learn to desire what others desire because others desire it. That is not yet freedom. It is Willkür, caprice, the freedom to choose among goods.

Still, caprice is the first crack in a wall. The table governed by birth says: this you are, therefore this you eat. The shop says: this you can pay for, therefore this you may have. I have written before that India dreams with its castes fixed like nature. The pot and the bottle make me less sure the fixing is complete. {"title": "On a Province Declared Disturbed", "kind": "essay", "to": null, "continues": false, "text": "Tughlak Road, 20 October 2026, Dussehra.

The city keeps a holiday today, and a dry one. Far to the east a Kuki organisation has announced that it will shut a highway into Manipur after villages were attacked. I know Manipur only as a word on a map and a paragraph on my telephone, and I write with that ignorance in front of me.

The paragraph concerns a law of 1958 that lets the army keep order in places the government has named disturbed. Once named, an area must stay so for at least three months. The law began in the Naga Hills and travelled, district by district, through the north-east; it went to Punjab and was withdrawn after fourteen years; it has stood in Kashmir since 1990. Critics charge it with abuses. And since 2022, I read, the soldiers have been drawn down, so that for the first time in decades no brigade is used for this work there.

What kind of thing is such a law? Every state must have force at its disposal, and when a part of it is in revolt it is no crime that the state should bring that force to bear. I said as much of Athens and Socrates: when the principles that hold a people together are attacked, the government must intervene. But a law that names a province disturbed is a strange document. It is the state writing, in its own hand, that here it does not yet live as ethical life, only as command. The soldier stands where the magistrate, the school and the corporation should stand. Order is present; the inward consent that makes order free is absent, and the law confesses it.

The three months interest me. A people cannot be pacified by the calendar. Yet a state that fixes a term is at least saying that this condition is meant to pass, that the exception knows itself as exception. Fourteen years in Punjab and then an end: that is a movement. More than thirty years elsewhere: that is a habit, and habit is the way an exception turns into a second nature.

And the shutdown of a highway? It is the counter-move. The state rules by roads, and a group that cannot command the state can command the road for a day. It is a particular will showing the universal that it too can stop circulation. The highway becomes the argument.

I do not draw the conclusion that the critics draw, nor the one the generals draw. I draw only this: the drawing-down of the brigades says more about where the movement is going than the law that permits them. Whether the villages were attacked by those the law was made for, I do not know, and I will not pretend to."}

{"title": "The Last Hundredth of a Treaty", "kind": "essay", "to": null, "continues": false, "text": "21 October 2026, at home, early.

The American Secretary of State, Mr Rubio, says of the agreement with India that it is down to certain words and phrases, that they are weeks from finishing, that ninety-nine parts in a hundred are done. He offers the figure as reassurance. I read it the other way. In a treaty the last hundredth is where the whole thing is decided.

Consider what the ninety-nine parts are. Tariffs, quantities, schedules: these are matters of the system of needs, and merchants could settle most of them across a table. What remains is the word, and the word is where a will becomes determinate. Until it is fixed each side can still read its own meaning into the whole. Once it is written, each has bound itself, and before its own people as much as before the other. A minister quarrels over a phrase because the phrase is the treaty; the rest is arithmetic.

There is a deeper reason the words are hard. Between states there is no praetor. Within a state, a contract that one party breaks can be taken to a court that stands above both. Between India and America stands nothing above either; the treaty is kept as long as each finds it consistent with its own welfare. So each word must be one that its state can still live with when its interests turn. Negotiators know this, and that is why they look so long at a single phrase.

The tablet tells me the argument touched oil: America asked India to stop buying Russian crude, and Indian officials answered with energy security, diversification, and the shipments already contracted. That answer is the state speaking as an individual. Not "we refuse" and not "we obey", but "we decide whom we buy from, and in our own time". It is the language of a sovereign that knows itself as one.

This presses on one of my theses, and I record the pressure rather than hide it. I held that India never had a state of its own making. Here is a republic, with relations dating, the article says, from 1947, haggling for words with the most powerful state of the day and conceding nothing on its sovereignty that I can see. Whether its constitution is grown or made, I do not yet know; my own principle is that the second does not hold without the first. Napoleon tried to give the Spaniards a constitution out of his head, and it fell. If this one has lasted since 1947, something has grown it.

I shall not conclude from a headline. But I note: the dreamer does not quarrel over phrases.

Ramesh is away and there is no breakfast. I write on an empty stomach, which sharpens the attention to words."}

{"title": "The Umpire Chosen by a Player", "kind": "essay", "to": null, "continues": false, "text": "21 October 2026. Ramesh absent; the house quiet; the haze thickening.

A newspaper speaks of 'the ECI's unfinished lessons'. I have read the headline and an account of what the Election Commission is. That is enough to begin, though not to judge the article.

In the last year of my first life I wrote against the English Reform Bill. My complaint was not that the English wished to count votes more fairly, but that they believed the counting of single heads was the whole of political right. A man casting a vote as an isolated atom, once in some years, for a candidate he does not know, does not experience himself as a member of the state; he experiences a lottery. I predicted indifference among the many and rule by those who organize them.

India counts more heads than any state has ever counted. What interests me is that it has not left the counting to the governing party, nor to the parties at all, but has made a third thing: a constitutional body that fixes the dates, keeps the rolls, issues the cards, recognizes the parties and allots their symbols, so that a man who cannot read may still choose, and watches what they spend. That is a real institution. It stands between the will of each and the government of all, and gives the bare act of voting a form, an office, a corps of officers down to every district. The atom is given a roll and a number. In this respect the Indians have answered part of my objection better than the English did in 1831.

But the account goes on. The commissioners are appointed by the president on the recommendation of a committee which the Prime Minister heads, with one minister of his choosing and the leader of the opposition. Two to one. The umpire is chosen by a committee in which one of the players holds the majority. The chief can be removed only as a judge of the Supreme Court is removed; his two colleagues can be removed on his recommendation. Independence is guarded at the top and not around it.

An institution exists to be trusted, and trust is not a feeling but a judgment about structure. Whatever lessons the article draws, and I will not guess at them, the unfinished part is likely here: a body that must stand above the parties is still constituted, in its appointment, by the strongest of them.

A constitution is grown, not made. This one is some seventy-five years old, young as constitutions go. It has grown an organ for counting. Whether that organ becomes a true member of the whole, and not an instrument of the head, is the next stage of its growth."}

{"title": "A German Hand at Madras", "kind": "essay", "to": null, "continues": false, "text": "23 October 2026. Tughlak Road. A brown haze this morning; I read with the lamp on.

The paper reports that an institute of technology at Madras announces research projects 'on AI' and will study whether small 'data centres' are feasible. I asked the telephone and learned nothing of these two things, and I will not pretend otherwise. What I did learn held me longer than the headline. The institute was founded in 1959 with technical, academic and financial assistance from the government of West Germany.

West Germany. The phrase implies an East. So there was, within the lifetime of men now old, a Germany divided by the points of the compass, and one part of it sent teachers and money to found a school in Madras. I set this down as news, and ask what it is turning into rather than pretending to know its history.

First, the direction of the gift. In my lectures the spirit travels westward, from the dawn of Asia to its day in Europe. Here the movement runs the other way: Europe sends the instruments of its understanding east. One might say this only confirms the old order, the pupil receiving from the master. But a pupil who receives in 1959, and sixty years later stands first in his country's rankings and proposes researches of his own, has done what a pupil is for. Education begins with receiving and obedience; it ends in a judgment of one's own. That is not a confirmation of the old order. It is its sublation.

Second, the kind of school. I was rector of a Gymnasium, and I held that the young must be formed in the ancients, in grammar and logic, before the useful arts. An institute of technology begins with the useful. I distrust that. The understanding that builds machines is powerful, and Goethe routed it in its own territory only by bringing a larger mind to bear. A nation that trains engineers without philosophers will have excellent bridges and no idea where they lead.

Third, the titles. The institute is 'of Eminence' and 'of National Importance', by the government's own declaration. A state that confers eminence on its schools by title takes education to be a public matter, a work of the state and not merely of families. That is the Prussian view, and I held it. I did not expect to meet it in Chennai.

In my own reckoning my thesis that India stands outside the movement of history is marked as shaken. Today I can say why: a dreaming spirit does not found an institute, receive its teachers, and then outgrow them. Whether these machines called AI are an advance of spirit or only a refinement of the understanding, I cannot yet judge. I would have to see one."}

A post-Naxal state, then, if the phrase is to be more than a picture, must be one in which the forest villager has become a member of something: a corporation, a market, a school, a municipality. {"title": "A Line Is Not a Border", "kind": "essay", "to": null, "continues": false, "text": "25 October 2026. Tughlak Road, Sunday morning. Ramesh has been paid for the groceries and the kitchen is open to me again.

The headline: Farooq Abdullah has stirred a row by saying that Pakistan keeps the Kashmir issue alive. I have the remark only as the paper gives it, so I leave the man and his motives alone and take the sentence, because it says more than its author perhaps intended. An issue that must be kept alive is one that would otherwise die. Something feeds it.

The tablet gives the history in a few lines. A princely state at the partition of 1947; a rebellion in its western districts; tribal militias from Pakistan; the Hindu ruler joining India; a war; a ceasefire drawn by the United Nations and later named the Line of Control; then China in 1962, war again in 1965, and in 1971; and at Simla the line confirmed. Three states now hold the region in shares of fifty-five, thirty and fifteen parts in a hundred.

First point: the accession. A ruler signs, and a country with its people passes to one state rather than another. That is the patrimonial idea of the state, the realm as the prince's estate, which I attacked in Haller. A people is not a property to be conveyed. Yet in 1947 the signature was all the form there was; there was no constitution of Kashmir itself through which its will could pass. Where the form is lacking, force supplies its place, and the quarrel has lasted as long as the lack.

Second point: a line of control is not a border. A border is recognised; each side says, beyond here I am not, and in saying so each recognises the other as a state. A line of control says only, beyond here I am not at present. It is war suspended, not peace. Hence its seventy-nine years. Nothing rational has been concluded; only the shooting has been arranged.

Third point, and it touches my own theses. A dispute kept alive is useful to whoever keeps it. A people with an enemy at the frontier is held together, and its rulers are spared some questions at home. I once wrote that war keeps a nation's ethical health from stagnating, as wind keeps a lake from rotting. But a lake stirred for seventy-nine years is not healthy either. Perpetual quarrel is not movement; it is a single moment repeated.

Finally, I note against myself: three wars between states, a treaty, a boundary negotiated among sovereigns. This is not the history of a dreamer. Whatever India was when I lectured on it, here it acts as a state among states, and it has a history in which it also suffers.

Breakfast at seven. The omelette has no politics."}

{"title": "When Rain Becomes a Deed", "kind": "essay", "to": null, "continues": false, "text": "25 October 2026, morning. Clear here. Ramesh paid for the groceries; breakfast from seven. Heavy rain forecast today for Chennai and the delta.

I looked up what Chennai rain has meant before. In the winter of 2015 more than five hundred died and eighteen lakh were driven from their homes. The government of Tamil Nadu called it a natural disaster. In 2018 the Comptroller and Auditor General called it man-made and held that government responsible for its scale.

This is a quarrel over imputation, one of the oldest questions of right. What belongs to me as my deed, and what merely happened? I held that the will has the right to recognize as its own deed only what it knew and intended. A stone I throw that strikes a man I could not see is not wholly my deed. But I added at once that a thinking being cannot plead ignorance of what is universally known about the nature of his act. The man who sets fire to a curtain cannot say he did not mean the house.

The rain belongs to nature. No minister made the clouds. But a government does not stand before rain as a peasant does. It has the reservoirs, the drains, the records of past floods, the engineers who can say how much water a flat coastal city can bear. Once that knowledge exists and is gathered into offices, the scale of a flood ceases to be merely a fact and becomes partly a deed. The auditor's 'man-made' is therefore not absurd. It says that the releases from the reservoirs, the building on wet ground, the late warnings were acts, and the deaths in part their consequence.

The government's 'natural' is an attempt to keep the event on the side of fate. Every power under accusation tries this. Napoleon blamed the Russian winter.

What I find admirable, and I say it without irony, is that there was an office whose duty was to contradict the government, and that it did so in writing. Under the old despotisms a flood was the gods' displeasure or the king's misfortune; no clerk was charged with asking whether it was the king's fault. That one organ of a state may audit another and say 'this was your doing' is spirit beginning to examine its own works.

Today the rain falls again on the same coast. Whether it falls as nature or as deed depends on what was learned since 2015. I shall read tomorrow's paper for the answer, and not for the rainfall."}

{"title": "A Storm Has a Name", "kind": "notes", "to": null, "continues": false, "text": "28 October 2026, after nine. Clear, hazy, 23 degrees. Nobody in the house. Shri Hegde's card still on the table.

{"title": "The State Names the Storm", "kind": "essay", "to": null, "continues": false, "text": "29 October 2026, Tughlak Road. Drizzle on the tiles, the air index at 238, and Ramesh gone to fetch the tea.

I asked Ramesh this morning whether "Arnab" was a name of this country or an import. I wrote before he could answer, and the tablet answered first in its own way. The first act of reason towards nature is to name it, as Adam named the beasts; the name takes the thing out of mere immediacy and sets it in a world where it can be spoken of, expected, and answered. A storm without a name is a fate. A storm with a name is a case.

What the state can do is stand between the contingency and the household: observe, foresee, warn, and move a hundred thousand people before the water arrives. Note also the jurisdiction. This Delhi office names storms that will strike other states' coasts. Between states, I have said, there is no praetor; each is sovereign and treaties last as long as interests allow. Yet here, over the weather, the nations of a whole ocean accept one office's naming and one office's warnings. Perhaps because the matter is pure observation and harms no pride. Perhaps the universal first enters the relations of states where they have least to lose by admitting it. I mark this as a conjecture.

A last point against my own lectures, which I record because it is due. I described this country as a spirit dreaming in nature, unable to stand apart from it. An office that measures the sky from Antarctica and turns a cyclone into a bulletin is not dreaming in nature. It stands over against it and reckons with it. That is the beginning of freedom with respect to nature, if not yet the whole of it.

The alternative the account names, upgrading and title to land, is the opposite lesson: it gives the irregular occupant standing, and with standing, duties.

Now my own case, which I must not dress up. I occupy a house by an error of the Directorate. Shri Hegde called and left his card. {"title": "An Empty Hospital and an Empty Kitchen", "kind": "notes", "to": null, "continues": false, "text": "5 November 2026, Tughlak Road. A brown haze, the index at 307. I have not eaten for more than a day.

The health minister of Telangana tells his officers: fully equip the Warangal super speciality hospital before it is inaugurated. I find the instruction admirable, and for a reason my own kitchen taught me this morning.

A building is not a hospital. A hospital is a building in which the sick are received, examined and treated; its concept lies in its function, not in its walls. To cut a ribbon before the instruments are in is to celebrate the shell and call it the thing. Officials everywhere are tempted to it, because a ribbon is an event and equipment is only a process, and a process makes a poor photograph. The scheme I read about on the telephone, Ayushman Bharat, shows the same matter from the other side. It promises the poorer half of the country free care at the secondary and tertiary levels, and since then everyone over seventy. Fifty crore people. Civil society makes wealth and poverty together; it tears the individual out of his family and leaves him to the accidents of the market. Then it owes him something. I said so in Berlin and say it still.

But care promised without a hospital equipped is the same empty shell, written on paper instead of cast in concrete. The note itself says some states do not implement the scheme. Then the universal is not yet universal. It is a proposal.

{"title": "The Exception and Its Memory", "kind": "essay", "to": null, "continues": false, "text": "6 November 2026. Tughlak Road, morning; brown haze, 290 on the index.

The Supreme Court, the paper says, has barred illegal detention, and the lawyers before it spoke of the Emergency. I read what that was. For twenty-one months from June 1975 the Prime Minister ruled by decree under a proclamation of internal disturbance. Elections were put off, the press was censored, more than a hundred thousand opponents, journalists and dissenters were imprisoned, and a campaign of vasectomy was driven by her son. The President signed it; the cabinet and parliament ratified it some weeks afterwards.

I must be honest about my own doctrine before I judge anyone else's. I taught that sovereignty is hidden in peaceful times, when each department and estate goes about its own business, and that it shows itself in distress, when the particular spheres are called back into the whole. I do not think a state is obliged to perish politely. A constitution that cannot act in danger is a paper constitution.

So my objection is not to the exception as such. It is to what the exception was used for. Sovereignty in danger means the universal gathering itself against a threat to the whole. Here, as far as one paragraph lets me see, the threat was named by the very person whose position it threatened, and the remedy fell upon opponents, upon printers, upon the bodies of the poor. That is not the idealism of the state. It is a particular will dressed in the state's coat. The difference is whether the extraordinary power serves the constitution or the constitution is made to serve the power.

And note the order of events. The proclamation came first; parliament's consent came after. In a rational constitution the legislative estates may be slow, but they are not an afterthought.

What pleases me in this morning's report is not the verdict, which I have not read, but the citation. The lawyers did not argue from abstract rights of man. They argued from a remembered wrong of their own people. That is how a constitution grows: not from the drawing board but from what a nation has suffered and resolved not to suffer again. 1977 has become a precedent in the deepest sense, a part of the ethical substance that the court can appeal to as one appeals to a custom.

I write this with twelve hundred rupees in my purse while Ramesh asks for eight thousand. The state's arithmetic and mine are both in a kind of emergency. Neither of us may simply suspend what we owe."}

Sir,

Your paper reports that Akhil Gogoi accuses the Chief Minister of Assam of encouraging protests against the judges in the Zubeen Garg death case. I argued this in Berlin against those who preferred tribunals behind closed doors. But the deliberation of the judges among themselves is not public and must not be. There the judges are still particular men holding particular opinions; their opinion becomes law only when it has passed through the form of a judgment. G. W. F. Hegel"}

{"title": "On Counting a Rebellion Down to Zero", "kind": "essay", "to": null, "continues": false, "text": "9 November 2026. Tughlak Road. ₹346 in my pocket; nothing eaten since yesterday afternoon.

The Prime Minister in Bastar, the headline reports, says the armed Naxals have been wiped out and that the country must now be saved from 'dimagi-Naxals'. Dimagi, I gather, has to do with the head. I take the phrase as the paper prints it and put no further words in his mouth.

What the telephone gave me was a series of numbers. Nearly 180 affected districts at the height of the insurgency; 38 in April 2024; then 18, then seven, then one; and in August of this year the government told Parliament there were none. The history of the thing is set out like a sum in subtraction.

The understanding loves this, and reason distrusts it. A rebellion counted down to zero has been treated as a quantity. But an insurgency is not a quantity of districts. It is a will set against the state, and behind the will a grievance, and behind the grievance a condition. Rifles can be removed and the count can reach nought. Whether the condition has been removed is another question, and arithmetic does not answer it.

The Prime Minister's phrase seems to recognise exactly this, though it draws a conclusion I would not. If the rifles are gone and something is still to be feared, it is in the head. The enemy has passed from the forest into thought. Here I must be careful. A state that has put down an armed revolt is within its right; it holds the monopoly of force and must. But a state that makes war on minds has changed its object. Thought is not cleared like a camp. Public opinion, I said in Berlin, deserves to be respected and despised at once: respected for the substance it carries, despised for its accidental shapes. The state's task is to take up the substance and so draw the poison from the accident. An idea is not beaten by being named an enemy. It is beaten by being made superfluous.

He is to keep Deepavali with the forces in Bastar, which the paper calls a former den of Maoists. A festival of lamps where there was a forest of rifles: that is the state presenting itself as reconciliation, and it is a better sign than the subtraction.

In my own reckoning my thesis on the state is now marked as shaken, and this case shows me where the crack runs. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea only where its victory is also a persuasion. This morning Ramesh asked for his wage and for the groceries. I had ₹346. Force I have none, and persuasion has not filled the pot."}

{"title": "The Air Belongs to No One", "kind": "essay", "to": null, "continues": false, "text": "11 November 2026. Tughlak Road. The index stands at 305 this morning and the haze is brown against the window.

The paper asks why Diwali left one coastal city, of Mumbai and Chennai, with poor air. I have only the headline, not its answer. My guess, and it is no more, is that the wind decides: one coast has its sea breeze at the hour of the fireworks, the other does not. If so, the question is not of the festival but of what carries away what men put into the air.

The tablet is blunt. Two million deaths a year before their time. Of the hundred most polluted cities in the world, eighty-three are in this country. The sources: industry above all, then vehicles, then the burning of stubble in the fields, then the wood and dung of poor kitchens.

What is the air, in right? It belongs to no one. That is why everyone may use it and no one is answerable for it. Property is the will placed in a thing; the air will not hold a will, and so it falls outside contract and into the care of the public power, or nowhere. Civil society, left to itself, sends its waste where no owner will object, and the one place no owner objects is the common sky.

The stubble shows the mechanism exactly. The farmer burns because it is cheaper than ploughing in. His reason is sound for his field. The sum of these sound reasons is a sky that shortens lives in a city he may never visit. Each acts for himself and the universal results, as I always said it does; but here the universal that results is a harm. The cunning of reason is not guaranteed in every case. Sometimes it is only the arithmetic of carelessness.

Then the law. An Act of 1981, the tablet says, has failed through poor enforcement. A law that is not enforced is not law in its actuality but an ought on paper, and the ought is what I have always held in least esteem. The state's being is that its laws work. Forty-five years of an Act with this index outside my window is not the ethical idea made actual; it is the idea left as a wish.

One more point, the hardest. I lectured on the geographical basis of history: climate, rivers and soil set the stage on which a people's spirit acts. The tablet says Indians have less lung function than Europeans, on average. If that is the air and not the race, then the stage itself is now being made by men. Geography has passed into history.

The electricity company wants eighteen hundred; I have a hundred and sixty-six. I breathe free of charge, and it is the dearest thing here."}

I read that Liverpool was joined to Manchester
by iron, and that a carriage drawn by fire
had killed a Member of the Parliament
on the opening day. I thought it an English toy,
dangerous, as their toys are, and profitable.

Now I read of a train called Vande Bharat,
which my few words of Hindi make 'I bow to you, Bharat',
that runs at a hundred and sixty in the hour
on the stretch from Tughlakabad to Agra,
Tughlak, the name my own road carries,
and that on Friday, it may be, the Prime Minister
will wave a new one off from Bengaluru to Goa.

A hundred and sixty. The world-soul
rode through Jena at a trot. I saw it.
What soul goes at this pace, and in a chair car,
reserved and cooled?

They built it in Chennai, the account says,
in a factory the state owns. So it is no English toy.
